::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 1) you can:

1. **model** a real system as a graph, choosing and defending the type — directed, weighted, bipartite, heterogeneous — as a modeling decision, not a given;
2. **construct and interconvert** the three storage representations — adjacency matrix, adjacency list, edge list (COO) — and state their space costs on sparse graphs;
3. **compute** degrees, the degree matrix, the Laplacian $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$, and walk counts via powers of $\mathbf{A}$, by hand, on small graphs;
4. **classify** any graph problem as node-, edge-, or graph-level and name a deployed industrial instance of each;
5. **explain** why node ordering is storage rather than information, and what that will demand of every model in this course.

Unsure whether your math and Python are ready? The ungraded
[Week-0 self-check](../self-check.qmd) takes ten minutes and names the
brush-ups.
:::

## A club splits in two, and a graph sees it coming

In the early 1970s the anthropologist Wayne Zachary spent three years observing a
university karate club — 34 members, and one slow-motion disaster: the instructor
(everyone called him *Mr. Hi*) and the club president (*the Officer*) fell out over
lesson prices, factions formed, and the club tore in half. Every member had to choose a
side.

Zachary had no machine learning — it was 1977. What he had was a record of **who was
friends with whom**: 34 people, 78 friendships. He modeled the split as information
flowing through friendships and predicted each member's choice from the network's
structure alone [Zachary, 1977](https://doi.org/10.1086/jar.33.4.3629752).

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Out of 34 members, how many do you think structure alone —
no interviews, no attitudes, no demographics, just the friendship graph — predicted
correctly?

::: {.predict-answer}
**33 of 34.** One member (ringed in red below) went against the graph's prediction —
Zachary even explains him: he was weeks from his black-belt exam and could not afford to
leave the instructor, whatever his friendships said. Every failure of a model should
come with a story that good.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-hero.html >}}

How he did it is a fossil record of this whole course. Zachary modeled the club as a capacitated network — friendships
as pipes, with capacities from how many settings each pair interacted in — declared
Mr. Hi the source and the Officer the sink, and computed the **minimum cut**: the
cheapest set of friendships whose removal disconnects the two leaders. His prediction:
the club would tear along that cut, each member staying on their leader's side of it.
No learning, no features, no probability — one combinatorial optimization on pure
structure, and 33 of 34 members landed where the cut said they would. Hold that shape
in mind: a quantity defined on edges (the cut), minimized over partitions,
predicting node behavior. §3 introduces the matrix that *measures* cuts; Week 2
minimizes it; by Week 6 a neural network descends from it. The karate club is the
course's origin story; we recompute it with better tools three more times.

That is the thesis of this course, in one 1977 result: **connections carry information
that lives nowhere else.** No column in a spreadsheet about these 34 people — age, rank,
years of membership — predicts the split like the friendships do. The information *is*
the structure.

Half a century later, the systems around you run on the same idea at billion-node scale:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w1-systems.html >}}

The scale is the point: Google's Knowledge Graph
reported five *billion* entities and five hundred billion facts in 2020
[Google, 2020](https://blog.google/products/search/about-knowledge-graph-and-knowledge-panels/) — every
search box query touches it. Pinterest's recommender propagates signals over a graph
of billions of pins and boards [Ying et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973);
Google Maps' ETA system, in production since 2020,
treats road networks as graphs and runs a graph neural network over them for a billion
users [Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11482). The molecule panel: the 2020 discovery of the antibiotic halicin came from a graph-level model screening millions
of candidate molecular graphs [Stokes et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2020.01.021)
— finding in hours what bench chemistry had missed for decades. And the quietest panel is the most universal:
every company's relational database *is* a graph wearing tables (foreign keys are
edges), which is why Week 14's "relational deep learning" may be the most
career-relevant session of the course. None could exist on spreadsheet features alone; all are
Zachary's move — read the structure — industrialized.

This course teaches you to **represent** such data (this week and next), to **learn**
from it (embeddings, then graph neural networks), and to **reason** over it (knowledge
graphs, up to the retrieval systems grounding today's LLMs). Today is the foundation: what a
graph is, how a computer holds one, the first numbers pure structure yields, and the
three kinds of questions you can ask.

**Roadmap.** (1) Graphs and their types — a modeling decision. (2) Three ways to store a
graph, and why the honest answer is "the cheap one". (3) First structure numbers:
degrees, walks, and a strange matrix called the Laplacian that will follow us all
semester. (4) The three levels of prediction. (5) The node-ordering trap — the deepest idea of the course.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
Only your prerequisites — nothing graph-specific:

- **BFS/DFS** from your algorithms course: how to traverse; we build on the *representations* they used.
- **Matrix multiplication** and what $(\mathbf{M}^2)_{ij} = \sum_k M_{ik}M_{kj}$ unpacks to — one proposition today turns this mechanical fact into a counting device.
- **Big-O** notation for space and time.
- From ML: features live in vectors; models eat tensors. Today's question is how a *relationship* becomes a tensor.
:::

## 1. What is a graph — and which graph?

::: {#def-graph .definition name="Graph"}
A **graph** $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ is a set of **nodes**
$\mathcal{V}$ and a set of **edges** $\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V}$,
each edge a pair of nodes. A **simple graph** is undirected, with no self-loops and at
most one edge per pair; $n = |\mathcal{V}|$, $m = |\mathcal{E}|$. Each node $u$ may
carry a **feature vector** $\mathbf{x}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{m_0}$, stacked into
$\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m_0}$. The subscripted $m_0$ is the *feature
dimension* — how many attributes each node carries — and is a different quantity from
$m$, the edge count; the unfortunate letter collision is standard notation.
:::

::: {.math-note}
Nodes are the entities, edges are the relationships, features are what a spreadsheet
would have told you anyway. The whole course lives in the tension between
$\mathbf{X}$ (what things are) and $\mathcal{E}$ (how things relate).
:::

Meet the graph that will star on our whiteboard for all fifteen weeks — six nodes, each
with its own permanent color, so that in any later diagram you can follow an individual
node through a construction:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-input-graph.html >}}

The definition above is the *plainest* graph. Real systems usually need more, and the
choice of *which* graph to build is a genuine modeling decision — arguably the most
consequential one you will make in any graph project:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-types.html >}}

Names to keep: **directed** graphs when the relation is one-way (citations, follows,
web links — a citation *from* a survey means something different than one *to* it);
**weighted** when the relation has magnitude; **bipartite** when nodes come in two sets
and edges only cross between them (users×items — the entire recommender-systems industry
lives on this shape, Week 14); **heterogeneous** when nodes and edges carry *types* —
the shape of a <span class="term" data-def="Knowledge graph: a heterogeneous graph whose typed edges are read as facts — (head entity, relation, tail entity) triples, like (Innopolis University, located_in, Tatarstan). Weeks 4–5 are devoted to them.">knowledge graph</span>,
which we treat as a first-class citizen of this course starting Week 4; **multigraphs**
when a pair can be connected more than once (two transactions between the same
accounts).

Each of those names deserves more than a parenthesis, because each one is a place
where a real project quietly went right or wrong. Take them one at a time.

**Directed graphs** are not "graphs with arrows added" — they are a different
epistemic object. In an undirected graph, an edge is a fact about a *pair*; in a
directed graph it is a fact about an *ordered* pair, and the two directions can carry
opposite meanings. A paper with ten thousand incoming citations is a classic; a paper
with ten thousand *outgoing* citations is a literature review. A Twitter account
followed by millions is a celebrity; an account *following* millions is a bot. Every
directed graph therefore has two degree notions — in-degree and out-degree — and two
different neighborhood structures, and any analysis that conflates them has already
made an error. When we reach PageRank in Week 2, the entire algorithm will turn out to
be a machine for exploiting precisely this asymmetry.

**Weighted graphs** attach a magnitude to each edge, and the modeling question is
*what the magnitude means*, because downstream algorithms will take your answer
literally. Is weight a **capacity** (road lanes, bandwidth), where algorithms should
sum flows? A **cost** (travel time), where algorithms should minimize sums along
paths? A **similarity** (correlation between stocks), where larger means closer? Or a
**count** (messages exchanged), where the scale is heavy-tailed and probably wants a
logarithm before any model sees it? The same number, interpreted four ways, feeds four
different pipelines. The karate club, incidentally, ships with edge weights — the
number of shared activities per friendship — and Lab 2 will step on this exact rake,
on purpose: many library functions silently *use* weights if present.

**Bipartite graphs** — two node sets, edges only across — are the quiet workhorse of
industry, because "who bought what", "who rated what", "who clicked what" are all
bipartite. One operation on them is so common it deserves its own warning label:
**projection**. To get a "products bought together" graph from a users×products graph,
you connect two products whenever some user bought both. Feel what that does to sizes:
a single user with 100 purchases creates $\binom{100}{2} = 4{,}950$ product–product
edges all by herself. Projections are dense, they weight hub users quadratically, and
they *destroy information* — after projecting, you can no longer tell whether two
products share one buyer or a thousand (unless you kept counts as weights, which you
should). Rule of thumb: model bipartite data *as* bipartite whenever your tooling
allows it (Week 14's recommender architectures do), and treat projection as a lossy
export, not a neutral convenience.

**Heterogeneous graphs and multigraphs** are what enterprise data actually looks
like: patients, doctors, drugs, and diagnoses are not interchangeable node types, and
"prescribed" and "diagnosed-with" are not interchangeable edges. You *can* flatten a
heterogeneous graph into a homogeneous one — forget the types — and sometimes that is
the right first baseline, but the types are signal: a path
patient→drug→patient means "shared medication", while patient→doctor→patient means
"shared physician", and a model that cannot tell those apart is averaging over
meanings. Weeks 4–5 treat the fully-typed case (knowledge graphs), and Week 10 builds
neural models that respect types natively.

Multigraphs — several edges between one
pair — appear whenever events repeat (transactions, messages, flights). Collapsing
them to a weighted single edge is the standard move, and the widget below prices the
standard information loss. Which brings us to **temporal graphs**, where edges carry
timestamps and the graph is really a process; we defer them to Week 14, but plant
the flag now: with timestamped edges, splitting data randomly instead of by time is
a leakage machine.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-multigraph.html >}}

One modeling honesty note before moving on: sometimes there is no graph until *you*
build one — practitioners routinely create k-nearest-neighbor graphs over plain
vectors, co-occurrence graphs over text, correlation graphs over time series. The graph
is then a lens you chose, and every conclusion downstream inherits that choice: a
k-NN graph with $k=5$ and one with $k=50$ can give *opposite* answers about community
structure, and a correlation graph thresholded at 0.5 versus 0.7 can change which
assets look "central" in a portfolio. None of these graphs is wrong; all of them are
decisions. We will return to this in the pitfalls.

::: {.callout-note title="A three-minute history: seven bridges, one abstraction" collapse="true"}
The founding move of graph theory was itself a *modeling* act. Königsberg, 1736: can
one walk crossing each of the city's seven bridges exactly once? Euler's insight was
not the answer but the representation — the landmasses matter only as meeting points,
the bridges only as connections; shape, size, and geography are noise. Two centuries
before the word "graph" existed, that is precisely the act you perform every time you
turn a database into `edge_index`: deciding which of reality's details are structure
and which are noise. (Euler's answer used nothing but degrees — the first graph
statistic, three sections early: such a walk exists only if zero or two landmasses
touch an odd number of bridges. Count the odd ones in the widget's badges. Degrees
start earning their keep in §3.)
:::

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-konigsberg.html >}}

## 2. Handing a graph to a computer

A graph is a set of pairs — sets are not tensors, and your GPU eats tensors. There are
exactly three standard ways to serialize the relationship structure, and you should be
able to write all three from memory:

::: {#def-adj .definition name="Adjacency matrix"}
The **adjacency matrix** of a graph on nodes $1..n$ is
$\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with $\mathbf{A}[u,v] = 1$ if
$(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}$ and $0$ otherwise — real-valued for weighted graphs, symmetric
exactly when the graph is undirected, and generally *not* symmetric for directed ones.
:::

The **adjacency list** stores, per node, the list of its neighbors — the representation
your BFS used. The **edge list** just stores the $m$ pairs; stacked as a $2 \times m$
integer tensor it is called
<span class="term" data-def="COO — coordinate format: a sparse tensor stored as the list of coordinates of its nonzero entries. A graph's edge list IS its adjacency matrix in COO form. PyTorch Geometric's edge_index is exactly this.">COO format</span>,
and under the name `edge_index` it is the representation PyTorch Geometric
[Fey & Lenssen, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.02428) — and
therefore this course's labs — runs on.

The construction is short enough to state completely — and Lab 1's first two
exercises implement it line by line, so read @alg-w01-edge-index as the spec you
will code against.

::: {#alg-w01-edge-index .algorithm name="Edge list → COO edge_index, with degrees"}
Builds the tensor representation the whole course runs on — plus the degree vector —
straight from a raw undirected edge list.

**Input:** undirected edge set $\mathcal{E} = \{(u_1,v_1),\dots,(u_m,v_m)\}$; node count $n$. **Output:** `edge_index` $\in \mathbb{Z}^{2 \times 2m}$; degree vector $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n}$.

1. $P \leftarrow$ empty list
2. **for** each edge $(u, v) \in \mathcal{E}$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;append $(u, v)$ to $P$; append $(v, u)$ to $P$
4. **end for**
5. `edge_index` $\leftarrow$ transpose($P$), giving shape $(2, 2m)$
6. $\mathbf{d} \leftarrow$ zeros($n$)
7. **for** each entry $u$ in row 0 of `edge_index` **do** $d_u \leftarrow d_u + 1$
8. **return** `edge_index`, $\mathbf{d}$
:::

Line 3 is the convention that trips everyone once: PyG stores an *undirected* edge as
*two directed ones*, which is why the tensor is $2 \times 2m$ rather than
$2 \times m$. Line 7 is a single `torch.bincount` call in practice — counting row-0
occurrences gives the true degree precisely because both directions are present.
Total cost: one pass over the
edges, $O(m)$ time and memory. Every loaded dataset should then pass the sanity
check $\sum_u d_u = 2m$ — the handshake lemma, which §3 proves.

The spec runs: here is @alg-w01-edge-index as live Python — edit the edge list,
press run, and watch the outputs track your changes (the first run fetches the
Python runtime; give it a few seconds):

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://pyscript.net/releases/2025.11.1/core.css">
<script type="module" src="https://pyscript.net/releases/2025.11.1/core.js"></script>
<div class="live-py">
<div class="live-py-head"><span class="live-py-dot"></span>Live Python — Algorithm 1 in your browser</div>
<script type="py-editor">
E = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 3)]  # undirected edge set, m = 4
n = 4                                 # node count

P = []                                # step 1
for (u, v) in E:                      # steps 2-4: both directions
    P.append((u, v))
    P.append((v, u))

edge_index = [[p[0] for p in P],      # step 5: transpose -> shape (2, 2m)
              [p[1] for p in P]]

d = [0] * n                           # step 6
for u in edge_index[0]:               # step 7: torch.bincount in the lab
    d[u] += 1

print("edge_index =", edge_index)
print("degrees d  =", d)
print("handshake  : sum(d) =", sum(d), "  2m =", 2 * len(E))
</script>
</div>
```

### Which one, then? Follow the money

::: {#prp-storage .proposition name="Storage costs"}
For a graph with $n$ nodes and $m$ undirected edges, the adjacency matrix stores
$n^2$ entries regardless of $m$; the adjacency list stores $n + 2m$; the edge list
$2m$. For a **sparse** graph — $m = O(n)$, the regime of essentially every real
network — the matrix is a factor $\Theta(n)$ more expensive than either alternative.
:::

::: {.math-note}
The matrix buys $O(1)$ edge lookup and the ability to *multiply* (next section); the
lists buy survival. Real systems store lists/COO and materialize matrix *products*
without ever materializing the matrix — you will meet this trick as "sparse matmul" in
Week 6 and live inside it from then on.
:::

Follow the money one level deeper — into what each representation makes *fast*,
because that, not storage alone, decides what production systems use. Four operations cover most of graph computing: **edge query** ("are $u$
and $v$ connected?"), **neighbor iteration** ("give me all of $u$'s neighbors"),
**edge iteration** ("stream every edge once"), and **matrix products** ("propagate a
signal one hop"). The dense matrix answers edge queries in $O(1)$ and multiplies
natively, but neighbor iteration costs $O(n)$ per node — you scan a whole row of
mostly zeros, which for a sparse graph is almost all wasted work. The adjacency list
iterates neighbors in $O(d_u)$ — optimal — but answers edge queries in $O(d_u)$ too
(scan the list), which is why systems that need fast membership add a hash set on the
side. The raw edge list is unbeatable for streaming and for building the *others*,
but supports neither query efficiently.

And the format the fine print of every graph
library actually runs on is a fourth one you should recognize on sight: **CSR**
(compressed sparse row) — the adjacency list flattened into two arrays, one holding
all neighbors consecutively, one holding each node's offset into it. CSR is the
adjacency list with the pointer-chasing removed: contiguous memory, cache-friendly,
and the input format of every serious sparse-matrix multiply. PyG's `edge_index` is
COO because COO is easy to *edit* and batch; the moment heavy computation starts,
frameworks convert to CSR behind your back. Knowing this saves you real debugging
hours later: "why did my model get faster when I sorted the edge list?" has a
one-word answer, and the word is CSR.

Two memory calculations to internalize, because they come up in interviews and in
capacity planning alike. First: Cora, $n = 2{,}708$. Dense $\mathbf{A}$ at 4 bytes:
$2{,}708^2 \times 4 \approx 29$ MB — fits anywhere, dense is *fine* at this scale,
and pretending otherwise is cargo-culting. Second: a mid-size industrial graph,
$n = 10^8$ users. Dense: $10^{16} \times 4$ bytes = 40 **petabytes** — not "slow",
nonexistent. Edge list at 50 friends each: $2 \times 50 \times 10^8 \times 8$ bytes
≈ 80 GB — a large but shippable artifact. The boundary between the two regimes sits
around $n \sim 10^5$, and "sparse or nothing" is a statement about which side of it
you are on, not an ideology.

Real graphs are dramatically sparse: Cora averages under 4 citations per paper;
ogbn-products, with 2.4 million products, averages ~50 co-purchases — meaning its
adjacency matrix would be **99.998% zeros**. Sparsity is not an inconvenience to
engineer around; it is a *fact about the world* (a person maintains ~150
relationships whether the platform has a thousand users or a billion), which is why
$m = O(n)$ — not $O(n^2)$ — is the safe default assumption for every complexity
estimate you will make in this course. Feel the scaling yourself:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-cost.html >}}

### The shape of the real thing

Sparsity is the first fact about real networks; three more will shape every method in
this course, and you should meet them before any of those methods, so that later
design choices read as responses rather than conventions.

**Degrees are wildly unequal.** Plot the degree distribution of almost any real
network and you will not see a bell curve — you will see a heavy tail: most nodes
have a handful of edges, and a tiny minority have thousands. In the karate club,
degrees run from 1 to 17 across just 34 members; on the web, from zero to hundreds of
millions. The practical consequences arrive immediately and never leave. A random
edge is far more likely to touch a hub than a random node is *to be* one — so
anything that samples edges (walks, Week 3; message passing, Week 6) over-represents
hubs unless corrected. Averages mislead: "the average paper has 4 citations" is true
of Cora and describes almost no individual paper.

And hubs are single points of both
efficiency and failure — remove the top 1% of nodes by degree and many real networks
shatter, which is either a vulnerability (infrastructure) or a strategy
(immunization), depending on which side you are on. You will meet this tail again as
"degree bias" in at least four different costumes this semester; it is worth one
minute now to see that they are all the same animal. Here is the karate club's own
tail — even 34 people suffice to produce it. The two dashed verticals are a
one-picture preview of a theorem §3 will prove:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w1-degrees.html >}}

**Distances are absurdly short.** In a graph with heavy-tailed degrees and a little
randomness, almost everyone is within a few hops of almost everyone — six degrees of
separation is the folklore version; measured values on billion-user social graphs
come out near four and a half. For us this is a *warning* dressed as a marvel: any
procedure that expands neighborhoods hop by hop (BFS, message passing) reaches an
enormous fraction of the graph within 3–4 steps. "Look three hops out" sounds local
and is not — on Cora, three hops from a typical paper already touches thousands. When
Week 6 builds models out of hops, the small-world fact is why *depth* will behave
strangely there.

**Closure is everywhere.** Real networks have far more triangles than chance would
give them — your friends tend to know each other. The karate club's members cluster
into tight knots; citation networks close triangles every time a paper cites two
papers that cite each other. Week 2 turns this into a number (the clustering
coefficient) and into features; for now it is one more entry in the growing case that
*structure is informative*: a random graph with Cora's size and density would look
nothing like Cora, and everything this course does is, in one way or another, a
machine for cashing in that difference.

## 3. First numbers from pure structure

Before any learning, the representations themselves already answer questions. Three
objects, all built from $\mathbf{A}$, will follow us to Week 15.

**Degree.** The first number you can read off the adjacency matrix:

$$
d_u \;=\; \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} \mathbf{A}[u,v],
$$ {#eq-w01-degree}

where — $d_u$ is the **degree** of node $u$, its number of neighbors; $\mathbf{A}$ is
the adjacency matrix of @def-adj; and the sum runs over all nodes $v$. Collected on a
diagonal, the degrees form the **degree matrix** $\mathbf{D}$. In the karate club, Mr. Hi and the Officer are
the two highest-degree nodes — the hubs the factions formed around. (Degree is the first
and crudest of the *centralities*; Week 2 builds the full toolbox.) Two bookkeeping
facts and one genuine theorem come free with the definition. Bookkeeping first: summing
degrees counts each edge twice — every edge has two endpoints, and each endpoint's
degree claims it once — so

$$
\sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}} d_u \;=\; 2m
$$ {#eq-w01-handshake}

always, where $m$ is the number of edges. @eq-w01-handshake is the **handshake lemma**,
and your fastest sanity check on any loaded dataset ("does the degree sum match twice
my edge count? no? your loader symmetrized, or didn't"). And a convention warning that
costs real debugging time: for directed graphs, some books define $\mathbf{A}[u,v]=1$
for an edge $u \to v$ and some for $v \to u$; row sums are then out-degrees in one
convention and in-degrees in the other. This course fixes $\mathbf{A}[u,v] = 1 \iff
(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}$, rows = sources; check any other source's fine print before
copying its formulas.

The theorem is the **friendship paradox**
[Feld, 1991](https://doi.org/10.1086/229693), and it is the heavy tail of §2 biting for
the first time: *on average, your friends have more friends than you do.* Precisely —
pick a random node and ask for its degree: expected value $\bar d = 2m/n$. Pick a
random *edge* and ask an endpoint's degree: expected value

$$
\frac{\sum_u d_u^2}{\sum_u d_u} \;=\; \bar d + \frac{\mathrm{Var}(d)}{\bar d} \;\ge\; \bar d,
$$ {#eq-w01-friendship}

where — $d_u$ is the degree of node $u$; $\bar d = 2m/n$ is the mean degree;
$\mathrm{Var}(d)$ is the variance of the degree sequence (zero only when every degree
is equal, which is when equality holds). The proof is one rearrangement — a node
of degree $d$ is an endpoint of $d$ edges, so edge-sampling weights each node by its
own degree, and high-degree nodes are oversampled by exactly their excess.

On the
karate club: $\bar d = 2 \cdot 78/34 \approx 4.6$, while the mean degree of a random
friendship's endpoint works out to $\approx 7.8$ — your average club-mate's friend is
nearly twice as connected as the average club-mate. Those are exactly the two dashed
verticals in §2's degree-distribution figure, and the gap between them is
@eq-w01-friendship drawn to scale. This is not a party trick: it is
the mathematical core of why random walks oversample hubs (Week 3 corrects for it),
why sampling neighbors is not sampling nodes (Week 6's SAGE must care), and why
immunizing the *friends of* random people beats immunizing random people. One
inequality, four weeks of consequences.

**Walks, by matrix power.** Here is the first genuinely surprising payoff of the matrix
representation. One term first, because everything propagation-shaped in this course
is built on it:

::: {#def-w01-walk .definition name="Walk"}
A **walk** of length $k$ from $u$ to $v$ is a sequence of nodes
$u = w_0, w_1, \dots, w_k = v$ in which every consecutive pair $(w_{i-1}, w_i)$ is an
edge. Nodes and edges may repeat — that freedom is what distinguishes a walk from a
*path*, and it is precisely the freedom that makes walks countable by linear algebra.
:::

::: {#prp-walks .proposition name="Powers of A count walks"}
For any $k \ge 1$, $(\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]$ equals the number of walks
(@def-w01-walk) of length exactly $k$ from $u$ to $v$. In particular
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[u,u] = d_u$, and for $u \neq v$, $(\mathbf{A}^2)[u,v]$ counts the
**common neighbors** of $u$ and $v$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (induction on k — worth doing once in your life)</summary>
Base case $k = 1$: $\mathbf{A}[u,v]$ is $1$ exactly when a length-1 walk (an edge)
exists, and a pair has at most one. Inductive step: assume $(\mathbf{A}^{k-1})[u,w]$
counts length-$(k{-}1)$ walks $u \to w$. Every length-$k$ walk $u \to v$ is a
length-$(k{-}1)$ walk to some neighbor $w$ of $v$, followed by the edge $(w,v)$, and
this decomposition is unique. Summing over the possible penultimate nodes $w$:

$$
\#\{\text{length-}k\text{ walks } u \to v\} \;=\; \sum_w (\mathbf{A}^{k-1})[u,w] \, \mathbf{A}[w,v] \;=\; (\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]
$$

— which is precisely the definition of the matrix product. $\square$
</details>

::: {#exm-walks .example name="Hand computation on the cast graph"}
On the cast graph (edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, CE, CF, EF$): $(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,A] = d_A = 3$.
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,C]$ counts common neighbors of $A$ and $C$: their neighbor sets are
$\{B, C, D\}$ and $\{A, B, E, F\}$, sharing only $B$ — so $1$: the single 2-walk
$A \to B \to C$. And $(\mathbf{A}^2)[A,F]$? Common neighbors of $A$ and $F$: $\{B,C,D\} \cap \{C,E\} = \{C\}$ — again $1$,
the walk $A \to C \to F$. You will verify all 36 entries with one line of code in the
lab; on the midterm you may be asked for two or three of them with a pencil.
:::

Common-neighbor counts are not a toy: "how many mutual friends" is the baseline behind
every "people you may know" feature, and in Week 3 it becomes the first serious
link-prediction heuristic.

**The Laplacian.** The strangest and most durable object of the week:

::: {#def-lap .definition name="Graph Laplacian"}
$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$: degrees on the diagonal, $-1$ for each edge off
it. Every row sums to zero.
:::

::: {#prp-lap .proposition name="The Laplacian is a variation meter"}
For any signal $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (one number per node),

$$
\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} \;=\; \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2 ,
$$ {#eq-w01-quadform}

where — $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ is the Laplacian of @def-lap; $x_u$ is
the signal's value at node $u$; and the sum runs over the edge set $\mathcal{E}$, each
undirected edge counted once. The quadratic form measures how much $\mathbf{x}$
**disagrees across edges** — zero
exactly when $\mathbf{x}$ is constant on every connected component, large when
neighbors differ.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (expand and regroup)</summary>
$\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{D} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}
= \sum_u d_u x_u^2 - \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} 2 x_u x_v$.
In the first term, each edge $(u,v)$ contributes $x_u^2$ once (via $d_u$) and $x_v^2$
once (via $d_v$); so both sums range over edges:
$\sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u^2 + x_v^2 - 2x_u x_v) = \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2$. $\square$
</details>

There is a fourth representation we skipped in §2 because it earns its keep only now:
the **incidence matrix** $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$, one column per
edge. Orient each undirected edge arbitrarily and put $+1$ at its head row, $-1$ at
its tail row, zeros elsewhere — each column is a little "difference operator" for one
edge. It is rarely how you *store* a graph (it is even bigger than the dense
adjacency for $m > n$), but it explains the Laplacian in one identity:

::: {#prp-incidence .proposition name="The Laplacian factorizes"}
For any choice of edge orientations,

$$
\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top
\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad
\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} = \|\mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{x}\|^2 ,
$$ {#eq-w01-factorization}

where — $\mathbf{B}$ is the incidence matrix above and $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$
is any node signal. This re-proves two facts at a glance: the quadratic form
(@eq-w01-quadform), since $\mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{x}$ is the vector of per-edge
differences $(x_u - x_v)$ and its squared norm is their sum of squares — and
*positive semidefiniteness* (PSD): $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} \ge 0$ for
every $\mathbf{x}$, because it is a squared length. PSD matrices return in Week 2,
where that inequality does real work.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (multiply one entry)</summary>
$(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top)_{uv} = \sum_{e} B_{ue} B_{ve}$. For $u = v$: each edge at
$u$ contributes $(\pm 1)^2 = 1$, totaling $d_u$. For $u \neq v$: only the edge $(u,v)$
(if present) has both rows nonzero, contributing $(+1)(-1) = -1$ regardless of the
orientation chosen. That is exactly $\mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$. $\square$
</details>

So the Laplacian is literally "difference, then aggregate" — the square of a
derivative-like operator — which is why it measures variation, why its kernel is the
constants (differences all zero ⟺ constant per connected piece), and why physicists
keep finding it in diffusion and electricity: it *is* the discrete second derivative.
The factorization also hands us a structural fact for free: the number of **connected
components** equals $n - \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{B})$, and your BFS from
algorithms class computes it in $O(n + m)$ — always the first statistic to check on a
new dataset, because many "mysterious" results (isolated test nodes scoring at
chance; embeddings drifting for one cluster) are just an unnoticed second component.
The sweep is worth writing down once in this course's notation, since we will call on
it casually for fourteen weeks:

::: {#alg-w01-components .algorithm name="Connected components by BFS sweep"}
Labels every node with its component id and counts the components — the first
statistic to compute on any new graph dataset.

**Input:** adjacency list $N(\cdot)$; node set $\mathcal{V}$. **Output:** component id $c(v)$ for every $v$; component count $K$.

1. $K \leftarrow 0$; mark every $v$ unvisited
2. **for** each $s \in \mathcal{V}$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**if** $s$ visited **then** continue
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$K \leftarrow K + 1$; $Q \leftarrow \{s\}$; mark $s$; $c(s) \leftarrow K$
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**while** $Q$ not empty **do**
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$u \leftarrow$ pop($Q$)
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each unvisited $w \in N(u)$ **do** mark $w$; $c(w) \leftarrow K$; push($Q$, $w$)
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end while**
9. **end for**
10. **return** $c$, $K$
:::

The outer loop guarantees no node is skipped; the inner BFS claims exactly one
component per restart, so $K$ ends up equal to the number of components. Each node
enters $Q$ once and each edge is examined twice — once from each endpoint — giving the
$O(n + m)$ bound, which on a sparse graph is simply "linear in the data". Note the
algorithm consumes the *adjacency list*, not the matrix: this is the §2 cost table
becoming practice.

Real networks typically have one **giant component** holding most nodes and a dust of
tiny ones; Cora's giant component covers ~92% of papers, and the other 8% are exactly
the nodes structure-based methods can say least about — remember them when they
reappear as outliers in Week 3.

Why care, this week? Because "how much does a quantity vary across edges" is the
mathematical form of the question the karate club answered: allegiance varied *little*
across friendships — friends chose the same side. That tendency has a name you will use
weekly, and it has earned a formal home:

::: {#def-w01-homophily .definition name="Homophily"}
A graph exhibits **homophily** with respect to a node quantity $\mathbf{x}$ when
connected nodes tend to have similar values of $\mathbf{x}$ — equivalently, when
$\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x}$ is small relative to what random pairing would
give. Its failure mode, connected nodes differing *systematically*, is called
**heterophily**. Read it as the single assumption doing the most silent work in graph
ML: friends share sides, papers cite their own topic — but fraudsters transact with
victims, and naive methods break exactly there.
:::

The Laplacian, then, is the instrument that measures homophily — that is what the
quadratic form (@eq-w01-quadform) computes. Next week $\mathbf{L}$ finds
communities; in Week 6 its eigenvectors become the *frequencies* of a graph and explain
what "convolutional" means in GCN. When a matrix keeps showing up like that, learn its
face early.

**The Laplacian's normalized cousins.** One refinement now, because it costs two
lines today and saves confusion in three separate future weeks. The plain
$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ treats a disagreement across an edge the same
whether the endpoints have two neighbors or two thousand — and in heavy-tailed graphs
(see §2) that lets hubs dominate every sum. The standard repair is to normalize by
degrees, and there are two conventional ways:

$$
\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2},
\qquad
\mathbf{L}_{\text{rw}} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A},
$$ {#eq-w01-normlap}

where — $\mathbf{I}$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix; $\mathbf{D}^{-1}$ and
$\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ divide by degrees and by their square roots (diagonal matrices,
so the inverses are entrywise); "sym" is the *symmetric* normalization and "rw" the
*random-walk* one. Read the objects being subtracted, because both will headline later weeks:
$\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A}$ has rows summing to one — it is a **transition matrix**,
"average over my neighbors", the exact operator a random walker uses (Week 2's
PageRank walks on it, Week 3's DeepWalk samples from it). The symmetric version
$\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ splits the degree correction evenly
between both endpoints, stays symmetric (so its eigenvectors behave, Week 6), and —
with one small modification you will meet as the "renormalization trick" — is
*literally the matrix inside the GCN layer*. Hand-check on the cast graph, row $A$:
$d_A = 3$, its neighbors $B, C, D$ have degrees $2, 4, 1$, so row $A$ of
$\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ has entries
$1/\sqrt{3 \cdot 2} \approx 0.41$ toward $B$, $1/\sqrt{3 \cdot 4} \approx 0.29$
toward $C$, and $1/\sqrt{3 \cdot 1} \approx 0.58$ toward $D$ — the hub $C$
contributes with the *smallest* coefficient, the leaf $D$ with the largest. That
inversion — normalization deliberately quieting hubs — is a design decision you now
understand three weeks before the papers that made it famous.

**What walk-counting is for.** Lest $(\mathbf{A}^k)$ read as an algebra exercise:
common-neighbor counts ($\mathbf{A}^2$) are the baseline behind friend suggestion;
$(\mathbf{A}^3)$'s diagonal counts triangles, which Week 2 turns into clustering
features; and damped sums

$$
\sum_{k \ge 1} \beta^k \mathbf{A}^k
$$ {#eq-w01-katz}

— "walks of all lengths, long ones discounted" — are Katz centrality, a Week 2
protagonist and the conceptual grandparent of PageRank. In @eq-w01-katz, $\beta \in
(0, 1)$ is a *discount factor*: a walk of length $k$ contributes with weight
$\beta^k$, so longer walks count geometrically less, and for $\beta$ small enough the
infinite sum converges (Week 2 makes "small enough" precise). Finally, the matrices
whose products a GCN computes are, as we
just saw, normalized relatives of $\mathbf{A}$, so a $k$-layer GCN's receptive field
is exactly the length-$k$ walk structure you can now count. One proposition, five
weeks of dividends.

## 4. Three levels of asking

Every graph-ML product you will ever build answers a question at one of exactly three
levels, and the level dictates the loss, the data splits, and the metrics — get the
level wrong and nothing downstream can save you.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-tasks.html >}}

Anchor each level to a system that pays salaries: **node-level** — integrity scoring at
every large platform (is this account a bot?), paper topics on Cora (our Week 6
running example); **edge-level** — "people you may know", product recommendation, and
knowledge-graph completion (which missing fact is true? — Weeks 4–5); **graph-level** —
molecular property prediction (the screen that surfaced the antibiotic halicin ran a
graph-level model over millions of candidate molecules), malware detection on call
graphs.

Semi-supervised framing, which will be our default: in the karate club, imagine you
observed the choices of only *four* members and had to fill in the other thirty from
the friendship structure. That — few labels, full structure — is exactly the setting of
Cora and of Week 6.

The level you pick dictates three engineering decisions, and it is worth previewing
them now so that when they recur weekly they feel like old acquaintances.

**What a "data point" is.** At node level, examples share one graph — they are *not*
independent, since neighbors leak information to each other, and that non-independence
is simultaneously the signal you want and the leakage you must control. At graph
level, each graph is a genuinely independent example, and classical ML intuitions
(i.i.d. — independent and identically distributed — splits, cross-validation) apply
almost unchanged. Edge level is the strange
middle: your examples are pairs, your negatives are *absences* (which, as Week 4 will
make painfully precise, are not the same as falsehoods), and the number of potential
examples is $O(n^2)$ while the positives are $O(n)$ — extreme class imbalance is the
default, not the exception.

**How to split honestly.** Node level: you hide *labels*, not nodes — the structure
stays visible, which is the point of semi-supervised learning, but it means a careless
feature pipeline can smuggle test labels through the graph (a theme with its own
dramatic episodes in Weeks 3 and 5). Edge level: you must hide *edges*, and every
upstream computation — walks, features, anything touching adjacency — must run on the
train graph only; violating this is the single most common broken evaluation in graph
ML, and Lab 3 will make you measure its cost in **AUC** points (AUC — area under the
ROC curve — is the probability that a model ranks a random true example above a
random negative one; 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect ranking). Graph level: split by
graphs, but watch for near-duplicates (the same molecule under two IDs) and for
covariate shift between collections. If your split has timestamps available, split by
time; the future does not leak into the past, and models deployed in production live
in forward-time whether your benchmark did or not.

**What to report.** Node level under class imbalance: accuracy flatters, use
per-class metrics. Edge level: ranking metrics (AUC now; Hits@K and MRR when we reach
KGs) because the task is "rank the true pair above the absent ones". Graph level:
whatever the domain demands — chemistry cares about ROC-AUC on rare actives. The
common thread: the level defines the population you are averaging over, and most
metric disputes are secretly disputes about that population.

## 5. The ordering trap

One more foundation stone, disguised as a bookkeeping remark. To write $\mathbf{A}$ at
all, we had to *number* the nodes — the cast graph's matrix came out as it did because
we chose $A{=}1, \dots, F{=}6$. Nothing in the club or the citation network chose that
numbering; storage did.

::: {.predict}
**Predict.** Our six-node cast graph can be numbered $6! = 720$ different ways, giving
up to 720 different adjacency matrices for the *same* graph. Suppose you feed two of
those matrices, flattened into vectors, to an ordinary MLP. Same graph in both cases —
does the MLP give the same answer?

::: {.predict-answer}
**No — in general it gives 720 different answers to one question.** The MLP reads
positions, positions encode our arbitrary numbering, so it learns storage artifacts.
Fixing this properly — building models whose answers provably cannot depend on the
numbering — is called *permutation invariance*, it is the deepest idea in this course,
and in Week 6 we will prove our models have it and catch an MLP failing it, live. For
now, carry the warning: **node order is storage, not information.**
:::
:::

Let us make the demand precise enough to use, because it will quietly grade every
method in this course.

::: {#def-w01-perminv .definition name="Permutation invariance and equivariance"}
Write $\mathbf{P}$ for the permutation matrix of a renumbering of the nodes, so that
$\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\top$ and $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}$ are the same graph
stored in the new order. A function $f$ that outputs one value per *graph* — "is this
molecule toxic?" — must be **permutation-invariant**:

$$
f(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\top,\, \mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}) \;=\; f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{X})
$$ {#eq-w01-invariance}

— renumber the atoms, same verdict. A function that outputs one value per *node* —
"which members join Mr. Hi?" — cannot be invariant (its output has an order too);
instead it must be **permutation-equivariant**:

$$
f(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\top,\, \mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}) \;=\; \mathbf{P}\, f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{X})
$$ {#eq-w01-equivariance}

— predictions travel *with* their nodes. In both displays, $\mathbf{A}$ is the
adjacency matrix, $\mathbf{X}$ the node-feature matrix, and $\mathbf{P}$ ranges over
*all* $n!$ renumberings: the property must hold for every one of them, which is what
makes it a real constraint rather than a convention.
:::

Two sanity checks you can run in your head:
the degree vector is equivariant (renumber nodes, degrees follow), and the sorted
degree sequence is invariant (renumbering cannot touch it) — so both are legitimate
features, which is why Week 2 can build on them. The flattened adjacency matrix fed
to an MLP is neither, which is the theorem-shaped version of the trap above. Every
representation this course constructs — centralities, WL colors, walk embeddings (up
to a subtlety Week 3 will confess), message passing — earns its place by passing this
test, and the one method that fails it will fail it in public, in Week 6, with a
seven-hundred-twenty-way contradiction as the exhibit. Run both checks with
your own hands before moving on:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w1-permute.html >}}

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reaching for the dense matrix because the formula has an A in it" icon="false"}
Formulas are written with $\mathbf{A}$; code should almost never materialize it. At
$n = 10^6$ — a small industrial graph — dense $\mathbf{A}$ is 4 TB. The formula's
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is computed from the edge list in $O(m)$. Translate math to
sparse ops reflexively; Lab 1 starts the habit.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Symmetrizing a directed relation without noticing" icon="false"}
Loading citations, follows, or web links into an undirected structure silently asserts
"X cites Y" ≡ "Y cites X" — destroying the entire notion of influence direction.
Libraries do this *for* you under the wrong loader flag. Know
which of your relations are truly symmetric; it is a modeling claim, not a default.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · “The graph is given”" icon="false"}
Someone chose those edges — a logging pipeline, a thresholded similarity, a k-NN
builder, a business rule. Different choice, different graph, different conclusions.
Interrogate the edge definition of any dataset before trusting results on it; when
*you* build the graph, report the recipe as part of the model. Even Cora — the
field's fruit fly — embodies curatorial choices about which citations count, and its
circulating versions differ enough to move published numbers by a point.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Judging a graph by its hairball" icon="false"}
Force-directed drawings of more than a few hundred nodes are decoration, not analysis —
layout algorithms invent geometry not present in the data. Judge graphs by statistics
(degrees, components, clustering — Week 2) and by task performance; draw only what is
small enough to read.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Assuming your graph behaves like the karate club" icon="false"}
Today's success story ran on homophily: friends chose alike. Transaction graphs,
dating graphs, and protein interactions routinely violate it — connected nodes
*differ* systematically. Every structure-based method you will learn assumes
something of this kind; the professional habit is to check it (Week 2 gives the
tools) before believing any result.
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 1](../labs/lab01.qmd) is the course onboarding: you set up the exact Colab + PyTorch
Geometric environment used all semester, load the real karate club and reproduce today's
hero figure's data, build the cast graph as a PyG `edge_index` **by hand** following
@alg-w01-edge-index (and check it
against assertions), compute degrees, $\mathbf{A}^2$, and the Laplacian in torch —
verifying @exm-walks numerically — and take a first look at Cora, the dataset that
returns in Week 6. Plus a two-minute detour into a real Wikidata fragment, so knowledge
graphs are concrete objects before Week 4 formalizes them.

A note on how labs work in this course, since this is the first: every lab is a single
Colab notebook with a pinned environment (the same one, all fifteen weeks — the setup
cell *is* the contract), exercises guarded by assertion ladders whose failure messages
tell you *what to check* rather than merely that you failed, and a couple of
predict-before-you-run prompts that are worth taking seriously — the thirty seconds of
commitment before executing a cell is where most of the learning condenses. The
assertions you see are the graded contract; run them as often as you like. Nothing in
any lab requires a GPU until deep into the GNN weeks, and even then free Colab
suffices — a deliberate constraint, because a method you can only afford to run once
is a method you cannot debug.

## Required reading

**1 · Battaglia et al. — *Relational inductive biases, deep learning, and graph networks* (2018).** [arXiv:1806.01261](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01261)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The position paper for the whole field: deep learning wins when architecture matches
data structure, and graphs are the most general structure. Read Sections 1–2 closely —
Table 1, mapping fully-connected/convolutional/recurrent layers to their relational
assumptions, is the single most important artifact; skim the graph-network formalism in
Section 3 on first pass (it returns in Week 6). There are no experiments — that is the
point: read it for the argument.
:::

**2 · Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec — *Representation Learning on Graphs: Methods and Applications* (IEEE DEB 2017).** [arXiv:1709.05584](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.05584)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The survey whose framing organizes this course: every method is an encoder + a decoder +
a similarity + a loss. Internalize that four-part template from Section 2 — it is the
mental filing cabinet you will slot DeepWalk, TransE, and GCNs into over the coming
weeks. Notice how today's task taxonomy becomes downstream uses of embeddings. Skip the
architecture details for now; we return to each in depth.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, §1.1–1.2 (definitions and tasks — our notation
follows it) · CS224W lecture "Introduction".

**Optional:** Sanchez-Lengeling et al., [A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural
Networks](https://doi.org/10.23915/distill.00033) (Distill 2021) — the interactive
article this course's style descends from; play with its widgets ·
Derrow-Pinion et al., [ETA Prediction with GNNs in Google Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11482)
(CIKM 2021) — today's road-network panel, deployed for a billion users ·
Ying et al., [PinSage](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973) (KDD 2018) — the
bipartite-graph shape at Pinterest scale; read the systems story, defer the math.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Modeling — A dataset of bank transfers: accounts, transfers with amounts and timestamps, some accounts flagged as mules. Choose the graph type and justify each property you keep.</summary>
Directed (money flows one way — symmetrizing destroys the laundering pattern),
weighted (amounts matter), multigraph or timestamped edges (repeat transfers between
the same pair are the signal, not noise), homogeneous nodes but with features
(account age, KYC — "know your customer" identity-verification — status). The task is node-level (flag mules) — and note this graph is
likely *heterophilous*: mules transact with victims, not with other mules (Pitfall 5).
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — On the cast graph, compute (A²)[B,F] and name the walks it counts. Then explain why (A²)[u,u] = dᵤ in one sentence.</summary>
Neighbors of $B$: $\{A, C\}$; neighbors of $F$: $\{C, E\}$; common: $\{C\}$ — so
$(\mathbf{A}^2)[B,F] = 1$, the walk $B \to C \to F$. Diagonal: a length-2 walk from $u$
back to $u$ must go out along one of $u$'s $d_u$ edges and immediately return along the
same edge, giving exactly $d_u$ such walks.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Representations — Your graph has n = 10⁷ nodes and m = 5·10⁷ edges. Give the entry counts for all three representations and say which you would use for (a) repeated "are u,v connected?" queries, (b) feeding a PyG model, (c) a whiteboard derivation.</summary>
Dense matrix: $n^2 = 10^{14}$ entries (≈ 400 TB at 4 B — nonexistent). Adjacency list:
$n + 2m = 1.1 \times 10^8$. Edge list: $2m = 10^8$. For (a) neither raw list is ideal —
a hash set of edges or sorted adjacency (binary search) gives fast membership; (b) COO
`edge_index`; (c) the dense matrix — on the whiteboard, $n = 6$ and clarity wins. The
representation is a tool choice per operation, not an identity.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Laplacian — Compute row A of L for the cast graph, and evaluate xᵀLx for x = (1,1,1,1,0,0) (nodes A..F). What is the quadratic form counting here?</summary>
$d_A = 3$, $A$'s neighbors are $B, C, D$: row $A$ of $\mathbf{L}$ is
$(3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0)$. The form sums $(x_u - x_v)^2$ over edges; $x$ is the indicator
of $\{A,B,C,D\}$, so only edges crossing to $\{E,F\}$ contribute $1$ each: edges $CE$
and $CF$ — total $\mathbf{2}$. The quadratic form counts the **cut edges** of the
partition — precisely the quantity next week's community detection minimizes.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Tasks — Classify each as node-, edge-, or graph-level: (a) will this user churn?, (b) is this new molecule soluble?, (c) how long will this road segment take at 6pm?, (d) which paper should this citation-manager suggest next?</summary>
(a) node-level; (b) graph-level; (c) edge-level (the segment is an edge of the road
graph — Google Maps' actual setup); (d) edge-level (link prediction between user/paper
or paper/paper). If you hesitated on (c): what is a node and what is an edge is itself
a modeling decision — road intersections as nodes makes segments edges.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · The trap — Your colleague trains a fraud model that takes the first 100 rows of the adjacency matrix as features "because the important accounts come first". Give two distinct reasons this is broken.</summary>
(1) Ordering is storage: renumber the accounts and the model's inputs — and answers —
change for the identical graph; "comes first" is an artifact of the export script.
(2) Even granting a meaningful order, row $u$ of $\mathbf{A}$ is an $n$-dimensional
one-hot-neighborhood vector: it cannot transfer to graphs of other sizes and treats
"connected to account #37" as a feature — memorization, not structure. Both failures
are cured by the permutation-invariant machinery this course builds.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Projection — A streaming service has 10⁶ users and 10⁴ films. An analyst projects the bipartite watch-graph onto films ("watched by a common user") to cluster them. One power-user has watched 8,000 films. Estimate that single user's contribution to the projection, name the two distortions this causes, and propose the cheap fix.</summary>
One user watching $8{,}000$ films contributes $\binom{8000}{2} \approx 3.2 \times 10^7$
film–film edges — likely more than the rest of the users combined, welding a near-clique
across almost the whole catalogue. Distortions: (1) density explosion — the projection
can approach $\binom{10^4}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^7$ edges, destroying the sparsity
every algorithm in §2 depends on; (2) semantic drowning — every film pair this one
account touched becomes "related", so clusters reflect power-user behavior, not taste
structure. Cheap fixes: keep co-watch *counts* as weights and threshold them; down-weight
users by $1/\binom{d_u}{2}$ or simply cap/drop extreme-degree users before projecting;
or best, skip projection and model the bipartite graph directly (Week 14). The general
lesson is the friendship paradox in disguise: pair-counting weights users
quadratically in degree, so the tail runs the result.
</details>

<details><summary>Q8 · Transfer — Zachary's model predicted the split from structure. State the assumption that made this possible, and describe a real network where the same method would fail badly.</summary>
Homophily: allegiance varied smoothly across friendships (small $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$
for the allegiance signal). A heterophilous counterexample: a bipartite
fraudster–victim transaction network — connected nodes are systematically *opposite*,
so "predict my label from my neighbors' labels" inverts the truth. Checking which
regime you are in, before modeling, is the Week 2 skill.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **Graph, simple graph** (@def-graph) — nodes, edges, optional features $\mathbf{X}$; everything else is decoration on this.
- **Graph types** — directed, weighted, bipartite, heterogeneous, multigraph, temporal: a *modeling decision*, not a property of the world.
- **Adjacency matrix / adjacency list / edge list (COO)** (@def-adj) — one graph, three storages; sparse regime $m = O(n)$ decides which survives.
- **Degree, degree matrix, handshake lemma** (@eq-w01-degree, @eq-w01-handshake) — the first structure numbers and the first sanity check.
- **Friendship paradox** (@eq-w01-friendship) — edge-sampling oversamples hubs; the heavy tail's first theorem.
- **Walk** (@def-w01-walk) — and walk counting by powers of $\mathbf{A}$ (@prp-walks).
- **Laplacian** $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ (@def-lap) — the variation meter (@eq-w01-quadform), its factorization $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top$, and its normalized cousins (@eq-w01-normlap).
- **Homophily / heterophily** (@def-w01-homophily) — the silent assumption; small $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$ is what "friends chose alike" means.
- **Node- / edge- / graph-level tasks** — the level dictates data points, splits, and metrics.
- **Permutation invariance and equivariance** (@def-w01-perminv) — node order is storage, not information; the deepest idea of the course.
:::

## Where this leaves us

You can now put a real system into a graph, store it honestly, and read off its first
numbers. What you cannot yet do is *rank* — which node matters most, which two nodes
belong to the same community, whether this graph is even the homophilous kind our
methods will assume. Structure has much more to say before any learning happens:
centralities that found search engines, a relabeling trick from 1968 that will turn out
to bound what neural networks can ever see on a graph, and the community-finding
machinery that Zachary's little club launched. That is Week 2: **classical graph ML —
structure as features.** Bring the Laplacian; it works there too.

Close the loop before you go — one minute, no notes: reconstruct the handshake
lemma and the check it gives you; the three storages of one graph and which
survives when $m = O(n)$; why $(\mathbf{A}^3)_{vv}$ counts triangles; the
friendship paradox's two averages (4.6 vs 7.8) and the sampling bias behind
them; and the invariance sentence — node order is storage, not information.
And keep today's three quiet theorems within reach as you go, because the whole
semester leans on them: the handshake lemma (your data-sanity reflex), walks-by-powers
(the counting device under every propagation method to come), and the quadratic form
(the cut-meter that connects a 1977 anthropologist to a 2017 neural architecture). A
course is mostly a small number of ideas wearing increasingly good clothes; you have
now met most of the ideas.

:::
